classification.difficultyReason: The displayed product suggests geometric expansion, but the proof must connect exponent choices to unique prime factorisations and justify complete, duplicate-free coverage of the sum.

content.prompt:
Let $\mathcal P_k$ denote the set of the first $k$ primes. Let $N_k$ denote the positive integers whose prime factors are all contained in $\mathcal P_k$. Prove that
$$\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\frac{1}{1-\frac1p}=\sum_{n\in N_k}\frac1n.$$

answer.short:
Each factor expands as $1+\frac1p+\frac1{p^2}+\cdots$.

Unique prime factorisation makes the expanded product contain $\frac1n$ exactly once for each $n\in N_k$, proving the identity.
answer.worked:
Write $\mathcal P_k=\{p_1,\ldots,p_k\}$. Since $0<\frac{1}{p_i}<1$, each factor is a convergent geometric series:
$$\frac{1}{1-\frac1{p_i}}=\sum_{e_i=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{p_i^{e_i}}.$$
Consequently,
$$\begin{align*}\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\frac{1}{1-\frac1p}&=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(\sum_{e_i=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{p_i^{e_i}}\right)\\\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\frac{1}{1-\frac1p}&=\sum_{e_1,\ldots,e_k\ge0}\frac{1}{p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}}.
\end{align*}$$
By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, every $n\in N_k$ has exactly one representation $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$ with non-negative integer exponents. The all-zero exponents give $n=1$. Thus every required reciprocal occurs exactly once. All terms are non-negative, so expanding and collecting them preserves the sum. Hence
$$\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\frac{1}{1-\frac1p}=\sum_{n\in N_k}\frac1n.$$
